sections.html: Hypancistrus contradens (L201a Big Spots) has large, bright spots on a deep black ground. The spots vary between white and orange-pink. A maximum length of 10 cm is given for the species.

This Hypancistrus comes from the lower Rio Ventuari in Venezuela – the largest tributary of the Orinoco – as well as from the Orinoco itself in the Ventuari estuary. L201, which looks similar but has much smaller spots, was imported earlier from the upper reaches of the Orinoco River. Exported species are often mixed, which can give the impression that they occur together in nature, which is not the case according to current knowledge.
No problem with keeping in groups, but only one Hypancistrus species to a tank as there have been reports of hybridisation.
Omnivores. Juveniles are keen on vegetable foods whereas adults are less so. Frozen foods such as brine shrimp, mosquito larvae and mussels, as well as tablet foods.

L201 has remained scientifically undescribed to this day. The large-spotted fish from the Ventuari was therefore called L201a in the trade. A "proper" L-number was never given to "L201a Big Spots"; it is superfluous, because L201a was scientifically described as Hypancistrus contradens in 2007. Nevertheless, the designation L201a will not be eradicated in the trade.

L471 looks completely identical and also originates from the Ventuari, but remains much smaller. L471 is said to reach only 5-6 cm total length (at least wild caught), while a maximum length of 10 cm is given for H. contradens.

Scientific papers only talk about standard length, i.e. body length without caudal fin, because one never knows if the caudal fin of a wild-caught fish is complete (usually it is not), while aquarium sources usually give the total length, including caudal fin. For example, the animal photographed has 8 cm standard length and 10,5 cm total length. As shown by the long interopercular odontodes ("whiskers"), it is a sexually mature male.

Hypancistrus contradens is a popular L catfish because its beautiful coloration remains throughout its life, whereas many other species become increasingly dull and washed out as they age.

Thought to be the original Hypancistrus inspector (which is L102) as shown in Aqualog and Datz as L201, but now named by Armbruster, Lujan & Taphorn in 2007 as Hypancistrus contradens along with three other species: H. debilittera (L129), H. furunculus (L199) and H. lunaorum (L339). Can be confused with H. lunaorum and H. inspector. This species was first introduced in the DATZ magazine, September 1995 issue, as L201, which is a different species with a more squat body shape. H. contradens has large white or pink spots that do not connect to form bands.

Etymology: The specific name contradens: contra (Latin), opposite; dens (Latin), tooth, referring to differently shaped teeth in the dentary and premaxilla.

IUCN Red List: This species has an extent of occurrence (EOO) of 10,870 km2 and a known area of occupancy (AOO) of 36 km2. It is possible that this species has been under-sampled in the upper Ventauri and the AOO may be higher. A decline in habitat quality is inferred, related to logging and illegal gold mining. However, there is insufficient information to count locations. Therefore, this species is assessed as Near Threatened (IUCN 2019).

Armbruster, J.W., N.K. Lujan and D.C. Taphorn, 2007. Four new Hypancistrus (Siluriformes: Loricariidae) from Amazonas, Veneuzela. Copeia (1):62-79. Echevarría, G. 2019. Hypancistrus contradens.
